rationale:
The incumbent was over budget in the article and five assessment fields, and the panel dissents, so this edition returns a complete assessment. It restates the judgment within the ceilings. The evidence has not changed since the incumbent. The case verdict stays contradicted, and the question, accounts, featured set and crux order are kept.

VERDICT CHANGES, each answering the panel.
- CCC-C001, well_supported to established (all five seats): critics reproduce the rings (CCC-E002, CCC-E008), and presence is agreed by every party.
- CCC-C503, CCC-C501 and CCC-C505 move to well_supported (the majority on each). As worded, each claim reports what was published or proposed, and CCC-E006, CCC-E007, CCC-E019 and CCC-E064 confirm the reports. The incumbent graded the underlying effect instead of the claim. The weakness of the effect now sits in diagnosticity (indeterminate or low) and in the objections.
- DECLINED: Grok's weakly_supported on CCC-C503 and CCC-C505, which grades the effect rather than the report. DECLINED: Gemini's established on the same three; one abstract-level record each is apt for well_supported.
- CCC-C504, provisionally_supported to mixed (adopting GPT and Grok). The source says each of the three regions covers no more than about 3% of the searched sky, so the claim's three-regions-in-3% overstates the concentration. DECLINED: the well_supported and established seats on CCC-C504, for the same reason.
- CCC-C509 to well_supported (four seats): CCC-E049 and CCC-E050 record the measurement directly. Confidence is moderate because of the 100 simulations. DECLINED: established.
- CCC-C005 to established (Gemini, Grok, Opus): the requirement and the concession come from the author (CCC-E015), and Tod lists fade-out as open (CCC-E016).
- CCC-C008 to established (Gemini, GPT, Grok): the theory described in its author's words (CCC-E018).
- CCC-C006, mixed to unresolved (adopting Opus). No record supports the entropy reset; one analysis attacks it (CCC-E017), and Tod lists related questions as open (CCC-E016). DECLINED: contradicted (Gemini, GPT), because it is a single analysis in a live dispute; the tilt against is stated.
- CCC-C010, well_supported to provisionally_supported (adopting GPT and Opus). 'Every signature' outruns the record while the ellipse and centre-concentration tests remain unrun.
- As a result, the component on the theory's physics moves from mixed to weakly_supported, and CCC-C505 leaves weakestLinks (replaced by CCC-C006).

HOLDS.
- CCC-C003 at well_supported (Gemini, GPT, Grok sought established): only CCC-E005 is attached, and artifacts and large-scale conditioning also drive the dispute.
- CCC-C011 at well_supported (Gemini, Grok): a universal negative resting on one table (CCC-E023), and DeAbreu et al.'s frozen parameters were a partial prespecification.
- CCC-C007 at well_supported (Gemini, Grok): the parameters are hedged, and 'decay completely' is an inference from CCC-E018.
- CCC-C519 at well_supported (Gemini, GPT, Grok): a single calculation that has not been reproduced (CCC-E042).
- CCC-C523 and CCC-C524 at provisionally_supported (Gemini, Grok): one paper, and its conditioning result, CCC-C512, is held on its source statement alone.

ARTICLE retold within budget, opening on the state of the question.
- Fixes: the ring-centre area figure is corrected. CCC-C502, CCC-C511 and CCC-C512 are now told as reports this site has not yet checked; the incumbent stated them as findings. The site's own internal vocabulary is removed.
- The plate is kept. The four accounts are told as in the field; the few-pixel account is told as its own account, though its claim link is the standard-model span.
- Cut to fit: repeated quotation, the polarization aside and the Ulhoa detail are left to the claim pages.

No research item changed status.
article:
Roger Penrose's Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) claims that our Big Bang was the remote future of an earlier universe, and that the earlier universe's black holes left marks on the microwave sky. Those marks would be [families of concentric rings over which the temperature varies unusually little, reported at up to six sigma]{claim=CCC-C002}, and compact hot spots his collaborators call Hawking points.

The rings and spots are really in the maps. So far, though, the evidence shows they are not unusual. Every independent group that has checked finds them just as often in simulated skies of the ordinary kind, and the headline significances fall away once the act of searching is accounted for. Two proponent observations have never been tested fairly: the rings' apparent preference for circles over ellipses, and the crowding of ring centres into a few patches of sky. The theory itself has not yet said precisely what it predicts.

## A universe before ours

Penrose, whose singularity theorems helped make the Big Bang respectable, published the theory in 2006, four years before anyone searched for circles. It starts from a puzzle: gravitationally, the Big Bang was extremely ordered, with very low entropy.

Penrose replaces “beginning” with “crossover.” In the remote future, after the last black holes evaporate, the universe holds almost nothing but massless radiation. To radiation, which keeps no clock, an eternity of empty expansion and a hot initial state look alike up to a change of scale; that is what “conformal” means. CCC takes this literally: [the remote future of one aeon becomes the Big Bang of the next, and the previous aeon's black holes leave their marks on our sky]{claim=CCC-C009}.

Colliding supermassive black holes would send gravitational shock waves that arrive as circles. Evaporating ones would leave hot spots. Unusually for a story about what came before the Big Bang, CCC makes claims about data we already have.

## Four accounts of one sky

**CCC's.** The rings are wavefronts from the previous aeon, and the hot spots are the last radiation of its biggest black holes. Expect true circles, spots of a set size, and a sky pattern that traces the previous aeon's clusters.

**The standard account.** [The sky is an ordinary realization of the standard cosmological model — inflation, then a universe of dark energy and cold dark matter, called ΛCDM — and the anomalies come from comparing it with a too-simple model of chance and quoting the best of many searches]{claim=CCC-C010}. Expect properly simulated skies to show the same features just as often.

**The large-scale account.** [The shortfall of variance in large rings is a symptom of the sky's known oddities in its largest-scale ripples]{claim=CCC-C523}, and [the crowding of ring centres into a few big regions reflects those same features, not scattered sources]{claim=CCC-C524}. These oddities are unexplained, but they predate CCC. Expect the ring anomalies to vanish in simulations that copy our sky's largest ripples.

**The few-pixel account.** A handful of freak spots a few pixels wide inflate the local variance, so the rings around them look anomalously quiet. Expect the concentric families to vanish when those spots are removed.

The last three are conventional and can all be true at once.

## The circles

{plate:IMG-CCC-P01}

[Quiet rings exist in the maps, and every group that has looked finds them]{claim=CCC-C001}, the theory's critics included. The fight is over a question that sounds too simple to fight over: compared to what?

*Significance* measures how unlikely a result would be if nothing interesting were happening. Gurzadyan and Penrose measured it against simulated skies of pure random noise plus instrument noise.

Within weeks, three groups ran the same search on skies simulated from the standard model, whose fluctuations are correlated across the sky: Wehus and Eriksen; Moss, Scott and Zibin; and Hajian, who also modelled the satellite's uneven noise. The circles appeared in those skies as often as in the real one. In Moss, Scott and Zibin's words, Gurzadyan and Penrose had “simply re-discovered that the CMB contains structure.”

The proponents accepted the fact and contested the moral. [Their critics “simulate maps using the CMB power spectrum for LCDM, while we simulate a pure Gaussian sky plus the WMAP's noise”]{claim=CCC-C003}, they wrote. They argued that the standard model's spectrum builds the disputed structure into “chance.” They also argued that concentric families “cannot be explained as a purely random effect,” a claim they never tested against standard-model skies.

Two later checks closed the remaining exits. Bielewicz, Wandelt and Banday scanned ring sizes from 0° to 90° around the two showcase directions and found no significant excess against standard-model simulations. DeAbreu, Contreras and Scott froze the search to the proponents' own published settings and applied it to the newer Planck maps. They found the special directions “at the same level of abundance in simulated Gaussian CMB skies.” Five independent checks reached one verdict.

Bielewicz and colleagues also offered a cause. They trace the anomalous ring variances to the sky's odd lowest-order patterns, its few largest ripples (multipoles up to ℓ = 7). They report that [the low variance of large rings around the main showcase direction disappears when simulations copy the real sky's values for those patterns]{claim=CCC-C512}; this site has not yet checked that passage against the paper. They judge the ring results “not consistent with the conformal cyclic cosmology scenario.” That judgment rests on reading CCC as predicting randomly placed centres, a reading proponents reject.

In 2024 Bodnia and colleagues, searching at full resolution, found the few-pixel trapdoor. Spots of “a few unusually bright … or dark … pixels, erroneously lead to regions with many low-variance circles.” Once those spots are removed, “no statistically significant low-variance circles can be found.” As the authors note, this explains false families around freak pixels, not necessarily every family reported earlier.

### What the proponents still hold

The strongest reply is the 2013 “sky-twist” test. Relics of spherical wavefronts should be circles, and [Gurzadyan and Penrose report that concentric sets drop off dramatically when the search looks for even slightly elliptical rings, and that ring sizes reach about 15° but never exceed 20°]{claim=CCC-C503}. The test compares the sky with distorted copies of itself, so the argument over simulated skies does not touch it. They did report this. But no one has run ordinary simulated skies through the same ellipse search, and how the test should behave by chance was worked out in the paper that reported its success.

The second argument is the sky pattern. [An, Meissner, Nurowski and Penrose report that about 83% of 1,134 ring-triple centres lie in three regions]{claim=CCC-C504}, which they read as superclusters from the previous aeon. Their text says each region covers no more than about 3% of the searched sky. The three together may therefore cover up to roughly 9%, not the 3% sometimes quoted. The large-scale account expects crowding of this kind, but that account was built on a different statistic and has never been tested on this one.

A Warsaw group also reported [ring structures in WMAP at 99.7% confidence against artificial maps with the same spectrum of fluctuations]{claim=CCC-C501}. A later paper [describes a Planck follow-up at 99.4%]{claim=CCC-C502}, a figure this site knows only secondhand. Both statistics were chosen after looking, by researchers who later co-signed the Hawking-points paper. Neither has been corrected for searching or repeated independently.

## The Hawking points

In 2020 An, Meissner, Nurowski and Penrose reported the second signature: [raised-temperature spots 0.03–0.04 radians across, with a size cut-off, at 99.98% confidence against 10,000 simulations]{claim=CCC-C004}. The five strongest sit at the same places in the Planck maps and the older WMAP maps.

Jow and Scott found that the 99.98% was quoted for the best-working spot size, chosen after looking. Once the sizes actually tried are accounted for — the *look-elsewhere effect* — the excess stands “at only an 87% confidence level (i.e., little more than 1σ).” About a third of what remains comes from the single strongest points. They also report that [dropping the two strongest raises the chance probability above 10%]{claim=CCC-C511}, a figure not yet checked here. The proponents had suggested that clustering of the spots would be further evidence, but [the thirty strongest are no more bunched than chance predicts]{claim=CCC-C509}.

López and colleagues built a detector that recovers 95% of synthetic spots made to CCC's description. It found “no significant ring-like structures” in four Planck maps, and they honestly report a small candidate excess at the 1% level. Bodnia and colleagues' machine-learning search also found nothing significant.

The matching positions in two instruments survive every critique, and they decide little. Jow and Scott found instrument noise negligible at these scales. Any strong real feature of the sky, ordinary fluctuations included, must then appear in both maps. Co-location shows the spots are on the sky; it cannot say which universe put them there.

A 2025 preprint by Meissner and Penrose, not yet peer reviewed, elaborates the signal rather than defending it. It proposes a “gravitational wave epoch” at the crossover, and a relation between each spot's temperature and the mass of its source cluster, which the authors say matches the largest clusters seen today. A signal's properties cannot count as evidence while its existence is in doubt. Still, this is the first quantitative prediction the theory has produced.

## Erebons: the prediction that reached a detector

Because CCC has no inflation, [the near-uniform ripples of the early universe must come from the previous aeon's dark matter, decaying during its exponential expansion]{claim=CCC-C008}. The theory names that dark matter: [erebons, particles of about a hundred-thousandth of a gram that feel only gravity, born at the crossover and decaying over “perhaps something like” 10¹¹ years]{claim=CCC-C007}, perhaps detectably.

In 2017 [Penrose proposed that correlated noise reported between LIGO's two detectors, at the same delay as the first gravitational-wave signal, might be erebon decays]{claim=CCC-C505}. He suggested searching at the delay of a nearby galaxy such as Andromeda. Nobody has, and two results suggest the search would find nothing.

First, Nielsen and colleagues subtracted the best-fitting waveform instead of the illustrative template the original noise study used. They find “no statistically significant correlations between the residuals.” Second, Bruce Allen calculates [the gravitational-wave background from such decays at about 95 orders of magnitude below LIGO's limit]{claim=CCC-C519}. Even the larger “memory” contribution misses “by 35 orders of magnitude.”

Allen assumed a smooth cosmic population. Galaxies are denser, but by factors like a hundred, not 10³⁵. The result leaves erebons as dark matter untouched. What it shows is that the detector prediction needs a decay mechanism that could actually produce a signal.

## The theory's bill, and its rival

For the far future to forget its scale, every massive particle must eventually shed its mass. This is [a “mass fade-out” Penrose calls “an admittedly unconventional hypothesis,” with no known physics behind it]{claim=CCC-C005}. The electron, which charge conservation forbids to decay, is the hardest case. Paul Tod, who worked out CCC's crossover equations, lists fade-out among the theory's open questions.

The entropy bookkeeping is also exposed. [Each aeon starts clean only if black holes destroy information and the crossover resets gravitational entropy]{claim=CCC-C006}. Eckstein argued in 2023 that information loss of that kind raises entropy instead, and no published analysis derives the reset.

The rival fits the sky with great precision. Planck's 2018 analysis matches the inflationary model to temperature, polarization and lensing data. Its one missing signature is primordial gravitational waves imprinted on the microwave background's polarization, and current limits leave many inflation models alive. A detection would point to inflation in our own aeon, which CCC abolished. That is the one place where the theory faces data it has not already survived.

## Where the dispute actually lives

No one disputes the sky; the contest is over method. [Across twelve searches from 2010 to 2024, on both sides, the signal model came from the searchers rather than the theory, and no significance, positive or negative, came from a protocol fixed before the data were examined]{claim=CCC-C011}.

Jow and Scott write that their conclusion could have been avoided only if CCC's predictions had been “made much more precise” in advance. The proponents answer that the critiques show “a more sophisticated analysis is needed.” The quarrel over whether CCC predicts scattered or clustered ring centres is the same gap seen from inside: a theory this loosely specified can be read either way.

The failing is not symmetric. A null result under the claimant's own frozen settings, which is what DeAbreu and colleagues obtained, outweighs a positive result that dissolves whenever a free choice is varied. But nobody preregistered anything, and that limits confidence on both sides.

## What would change our mind

The decisive project is desk work on public data. Both camps would endorse a protocol before anyone looks — statistic, simulated skies, mask, few-pixel screen, look-elsewhere correction, all frozen — and it would be applied once to the final Planck maps. Either outcome would settle the existing claims. Narrower tests decide among the accounts:

- **A fair ellipse test.** Run simulated ordinary skies through the sky-twist search. If the real sky prefers circles and the simulations do not, the proponents' best argument stands. If the simulations show the same drop-off, it falls.
- **Ring centres against matched skies.** Repeat the ring-centre count on standard simulations and on simulations that copy our sky's largest ripples. If the matched skies routinely crowd about 80% of centres into three regions, the large-scale account wins. If neither kind comes close, the crowding becomes the strongest surviving proponent observation.
- **Quantitative predictions.** How many circles, how faint, what shape; how many spots, how bright, where. Until the theory says, positive claims cannot be credited and null results cannot be fatal.

Beyond the microwave maps:

- A detection of primordial gravitational waves would count against CCC.
- An erebon decay mechanism that yields a computable signal at a detector would reopen the LIGO route; a proof that none can would close it.
- A working mass fade-out, or a proof that one is impossible, would reshape the theory whatever the sky shows.

The universe before this one is not a foolish idea. It is a serious idea whose observational case has so far failed review, stuck at an impasse that is methodological rather than cosmic. The sky is not going anywhere. What the case waits for is a protocol, and a theory precise enough to be bound by one.

assessment.synthesis:
The features are real; the anomaly and the attribution fail.

Critics reproduce the low-variance rings on WMAP and Planck (CCC-E002, CCC-E008, for CCC-C001).

The circle anomaly (CCC-C002) is contradicted two ways:
- five independent reanalyses find chance abundance against standard-model skies (CCC-E002, CCC-E003, CCC-E004, CCC-E037, CCC-E008);
- a few-pixel mechanism manufactures concentric sets (CCC-E012).

The Hawking-point anomaly (CCC-C004) fails on three counts:
- it falls from 99.98% to 87% under size marginalization (CCC-E010);
- it draws a third of its residue from single points (CCC-E054);
- it is absent both in a detector validated on synthetic CCC spots (CCC-E011) and at full resolution (CCC-E012).

The proponents' own response documents the comparison-sky crux (CCC-E005, for CCC-C003).

With both anomalies gone, the attribution (CCC-C009) is contradicted. Bielewicz et al.'s inconsistency argument (CCC-E058, CCC-E059, CCC-E060) adds weight but rests on a disputed reading of CCC. The 2025 preprint (CCC-E022) elaborates an unrehabilitated signal.

The conventional account (CCC-C010) is strongly evidenced (CCC-E003, CCC-E010, CCC-E012, CCC-E056). It is graded provisional because 'every signature' outruns the record: the reported ellipse preference (CCC-C503, per CCC-E006) and the centre concentration (CCC-C504) have never met a fair null. Bielewicz et al. supply a low-multipole cause for large-radius deficits and regional clustering (CCC-E056, CCC-E057, for CCC-C523 and CCC-C524).

The erebon route adds nothing. Penrose's LIGO proposal is accurately reported (CCC-C505), but its premise fails on a maximum-likelihood analysis, and the memory background misses detectability by 35 orders (CCC-E067, CCC-E069). The direct background misses by 95 (CCC-E042, for CCC-C519).

No search on either side was preregistered (CCC-E023), which caps the critical case too.

Sensitivity: removing CCC-E012 would most change the verdict, as the only record reaching both signatures with a false-positive mechanism. Without it, CCC-E002, CCC-E003, CCC-E004, CCC-E008 and CCC-E037 on the circles, and CCC-E010, CCC-E011 and CCC-E054 on the Hawking points, still sustain 'contradicted'.

The mechanism grades (CCC-C005, CCC-C006) lean partly on priors about charge conservation and unitarity. The verdict concerns the detection claims, not CCC as a cosmology, which remains untested.
assessment.steelman:
Two proponent observations have never met a fair test, and neither depends on the disputed comparison skies.

First, Gurzadyan and Penrose report that concentric low-variance sets become far rarer when the search looks for even slightly elliptical rings, and that ring radii stop near 15–20° (CCC-C503, recorded in CCC-E006). Proponents read this as the signature of spherical wavefronts, which a generic search artifact has no evident reason to prefer.

Second, An et al. report that about 83% of 1134 ring-triple centres fall within three regions, each no more than about 3% of the searched sky (CCC-C504). Proponents read this as previous-aeon superclusters. The low-multipole account offered for such clustering (CCC-C524) was established on a different statistic and never tested on this one.

Three further points strengthen the case:
- the framework was published four years before any search (CCC-E014);
- the Hawking-point residue after correction is 87% rather than zero (CCC-E010);
- every null was aimed at a signal model the searchers had to invent (CCC-E023).

From these a proponent can argue that the searches have tested guesses about CCC, not CCC itself. None of this revives the anomaly claims; it is why the ellipse and centre-concentration tests lead the agenda.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: Roger Penrose's Conformal Cyclic Cosmology holds that our Big Bang was the remote future of a previous universe, whose black-hole collisions and evaporations left marks on our microwave sky. Proponents report concentric rings of unusually steady temperature (up to 6σ) and compact hot 'Hawking points' (99.98% confidence) in the WMAP and Planck maps, and read them as those marks.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: The dispute is over what counts as chance: the features are real, but whether they are surprising depends on the comparison skies and on correcting for having searched. Proponents compared against plain random skies. Five independent reanalyses, using skies simulated from the standard model, find the rings just as often. Correcting for the spot sizes tried cuts the Hawking-point confidence to about 87%. Still untested: the rings' reported preference for circles over ellipses, and the crowding of ring centres.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A protocol both camps agree and freeze before looking — statistic, comparison skies, artifact screen, search correction — applied once to the final Planck maps would settle the detection claims. Two cheaper tests decide between accounts: do simulated skies show the same circle-over-ellipse preference, and do skies copying our sky's largest ripples reproduce the ring-centre crowding? A detection of primordial gravitational waves would count against CCC itself.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation:
The microwave sky is a random field whose fluctuations are correlated as the standard inflationary model (ΛCDM) predicts. Such a field is full of structure, including quiet rings and warm spots at the abundance the reanalyses find.

The high significances came from three sources:
- comparing the sky with plain random skies that lack those correlations;
- choosing statistics and sizes after looking;
- a few freak pixels that generate concentric quiet rings around themselves.

The large-radius shortfall and the regional clustering of ring centres reflect the sky's known, unexplained oddities at its largest scales, which predate CCC. The Planck–WMAP co-location of the strongest spots is expected for any real sky feature once instrument noise is negligible.

Two items are not yet explained so much as untested: the reported circle-over-ellipse preference and the specific ring-centre concentration.

components.label: The concentric circles
components.note: The rings are real and reproduced; five independent checks find them at chance abundance, and freak pixels and large-scale oddities explain them. The ellipse preference and centre crowding remain untested.

components.label: The Hawking points
components.note: 99.98% falls to about 87% once spot size is not chosen after looking; a third of the excess sits in single points; two independent searches find no significant population.

components.label: What counts as chance
components.note: Both camps state in print that the disagreement is the comparison sky; no search on either side was preregistered, and every signal model was invented by the searchers.

components.label: The theory's physics
components.note: Mass fade-out is required, conceded unconventional and has no mechanism; the entropy reset has no supporting analysis and one published critique.

components.label: Erebons and the detector prediction
components.note: A genuine forward prediction, but the LIGO-noise premise fails on a better analysis and the only calculation puts the signal 35–95 orders of magnitude below detectability.

components.label: The standard inflationary model
components.note: Fits the sky precisely; its one missing signature, primordial gravitational waves, is the measurement that could count against CCC.

researchPriority.reason: Cheap desk tests on public data could close or reopen the case: a preregistered joint reanalysis, a fair ellipse test, and a ring-centre test against large-scale-matched skies. No live anomaly demands urgency.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The attribution depends on the anomaly claims CCC-C002 and CCC-C004, both contradicted. The proponents' detections attached here (CCC-E001, CCC-E009) are undercut by the reanalyses of those claims. Bielewicz et al. judge the ring properties inconsistent with CCC (CCC-E058, CCC-E059, CCC-E060), though on a reading of CCC's prediction that proponents dispute. The 2025 preprint (CCC-E022) elaborates a signal whose existence is unrehabilitated. The framework's priority (CCC-E014) shows the theory was not fitted after the fact, but it supplies no significance.

treatment.plainLanguage: The central thesis: that the rings and hot spots are scars from a universe before ours. Once the rings and spots turn out to be ordinary, nothing is left for this reading to explain.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis itself; its fate follows from whether the features are anomalous at all (CCC-C002, CCC-C004).
treatment.strongestObjection: The theory predates the searches (CCC-E014), and two structural observations, the ellipse preference and the centre crowding, have never been tested against a fair null.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A jointly preregistered reanalysis of the final Planck maps that finds a surviving excess
A fair ellipse test in which the real sky prefers circles and simulated skies do not
A quantitative CCC prediction, fixed in advance, confirmed in the data

treatment.plainLanguage: The rival account: an ordinary sky plus the statistics of searching explains every reported signature. It explains most of them; two have not yet been checked.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The direct competitor to the thesis; where it holds, the previous-aeon reading has nothing left to explain.
treatment.strongestObjection: 'Every' outruns the record: the ellipse preference and centre crowding are untested, and an 87% residue and a 1%-level candidate excess remain.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Fair-null tests of the ellipse preference and centre crowding that the real sky passes and the simulations fail
A preregistered search finding a Hawking-point population that survives artifact screening

treatment.plainLanguage: The claim that the ring families are too common to be chance. Independent checks find them just as common in simulated ordinary skies.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, it would be the anomaly CCC needs; its failure removes the circles' support for the thesis.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every reanalysis builds the standard model's correlations into its comparison skies, the very choice proponents dispute (CCC-E005).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered reanalysis with artifact screening that still finds an excess
A demonstration that standard-model comparison skies smuggle in the signal being tested

claimAssessments.reasoning: The 99.98% was quoted for the best ring size; marginalizing over the sizes searched gives 87%, about 1σ (CCC-E010). A third of the excess comes from single points (CCC-E054). López et al.'s detector, which recovers 95% of synthetic CCC spots, finds no significant population (CCC-E011), and HawkingNet finds none (CCC-E012). Instrument noise is negligible at these scales (CCC-E028), so the Planck–WMAP co-location in CCC-E009 shows the spots are on the sky, not where they came from. CCC-E023: no search was preregistered.

treatment.plainLanguage: The claim that compact hot spots of a set size are too frequent to be chance. Correcting for the spot sizes that were tried removes almost all of the significance.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The program's strongest recent anomaly claim; its failure removes the second pillar of the attribution.
treatment.strongestObjection: The 87% residue and López et al.'s 1%-level candidate excess are not zero, and the two-instrument co-location of the strongest spots stands (though it is expected for any real sky feature).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A search with a spot profile fixed in advance from CCC that finds an excess after look-elsewhere correction
Independent confirmation of the 2025 mass–temperature relation on a preregistered spot sample

claimAssessments.reasoning: Independent critics explicitly reproduce the ring structures and verify the procedure (CCC-E002). DeAbreu et al. confirm the special directions in Planck as well as WMAP (CCC-E008), and the proponents' detection reports them (CCC-E001). This adopts the unanimous panel dissent: presence and reproducibility are agreed by every party. Bodnia et al.'s few-pixel diagnosis bears on the rings' cause, not their presence.

treatment.plainLanguage: Rings of unusually steady temperature really are in the microwave maps; everyone who looks finds them.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both CCC and the standard model predict such features, so their existence separates nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: Some reproduced concentric sets are generated by freak pixels rather than by any coherent ring (the few-pixel diagnosis).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A careful reanalysis failing to reproduce the rings with the published procedure

claimAssessments.reasoning: The proponents' own response states the difference: critics simulate skies with the standard model's power spectrum, while they simulate a pure Gaussian sky plus noise (CCC-E005). The reanalyses logged under CCC-C002 find the features typical under the former. This holds against three seats that sought established. Only one record is attached, and later disputes add artifact screening and large-scale conditioning, so the ensemble is the central source of disagreement but not the only one.

treatment.plainLanguage: Why the two sides disagree: they compared the sky with different kinds of simulated 'chance' sky.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It locates the circle significance dispute; whoever is right about the comparison sky wins the circles.
treatment.strongestObjection: Proponents argue that the standard-model spectrum builds the disputed structure into 'chance', an argument never quantified (CCC-E005).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A quantified proponent demonstration that concentric families are rare even in standard-model skies
Evidence that masks or noise modelling, not the ensemble, drive the difference

claimAssessments.reasoning: The study table finds that across twelve searches (2010–2024) the signal model was supplied by the searchers, and no significance came from a protocol fixed in advance (CCC-E023). Jow & Scott note that only a precise prior prediction could have escaped their correction (CCC-E055). The proponents treat nulls as calls for better analysis (CCC-E013), and the 2025 preprint offers the first derived fragment of a signal model (CCC-E022). Held short of established against two seats: this is a universal negative resting on one table, and DeAbreu et al.'s frozen parameters were a partial prespecification.

treatment.plainLanguage: No one on either side fixed their methods before looking at the data.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Caps confidence on both sides without favouring either; it explains why the dispute persists.
treatment.strongestObjection: A null under the claimant's own published parameters (DeAbreu et al.) comes close to a prespecified test.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A published search whose protocol was deposited before its analysis

claimAssessments.reasoning: As worded, the claim reports what Gurzadyan and Penrose published. Their refereed abstract states both parts: set counts drop dramatically with ellipticity, and radii reach about 15° but none exceed 20° (CCC-E006). This adopts the panel majority; the incumbent's 'unresolved' graded the effect, not the report. Whether the effect is real is untested: the statistic and its expected behaviour were introduced in the same paper, and no independent group has re-run it with an ellipse-specific null.

treatment.plainLanguage: Penrose and Gurzadyan reported that the ring sets largely vanish if you look for slightly oval rings instead of circles. The report is accurate; nobody has checked whether ordinary skies do the same.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Potentially the most diagnostic proponent observation, but its weight cannot be judged until simulated skies are run through the same test (CCC-E006).
treatment.strongestObjection: The test was designed and scored in the paper that reported its success, and few-pixel artifacts could interact with it in ways nobody has assessed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Simulated standard-model skies run through the same ellipse search showing no circle preference (would make it strong for CCC)
Simulated skies showing the same drop-off (would neutralize it)

claimAssessments.reasoning: The proponents' paper reports that about 83% of 1134 triple centres lie within three regions, but its text says each region covers no more than about 3% of the searched sky. The claim's 'three regions covering roughly 3%' therefore overstates the concentration; the source allows up to roughly three times that area. A qualitatively anisotropic distribution was also reported in 2013 (CCC-E006). Bielewicz et al. offer large-scale features as a cause of such clustering, on a different statistic (CCC-E061). This adopts the GPT and Grok dissents.

treatment.plainLanguage: Proponents report that most ring centres crowd into three small patches of sky. They did report this, but each patch covers up to 3% of the sky, not all three together.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It would favour one account only once skies copying our largest-scale ripples are run through the same count.
treatment.strongestObjection: The conventional large-scale account expected clustering in a few large regions before this figure was published (CCC-E061).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The full text's area figures read and checked
Large-scale-matched simulations routinely reaching about 80% concentration (neutralizes it) or never approaching it (strengthens it)

claimAssessments.reasoning: The refereed abstract states the 99.7% result against artificial maps of the same harmonic content (CCC-E007), so the report is accurate. This adopts the panel's upgrade from weakly supported, which graded the effect rather than the report. As evidence for an anomaly it is weak: the group later co-authored with Penrose, the statistic and threshold were chosen after looking, and there is no look-elsewhere correction or independent replication.

treatment.plainLanguage: A Warsaw group reported ring structures at 99.7% confidence. They did; the figure has never been independently checked or corrected for searching.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A post-hoc statistic from a group close to the proponents; figures of this kind dissolve under correction elsewhere in the case.
treatment.strongestObjection: Comparison maps with the same harmonic content preserve the power spectrum, which partly meets the critics' ensemble objection.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent replication of this statistic with a look-elsewhere correction

claimAssessments.reasoning: Jow & Scott's 100 simulations give a mean nearest-neighbour distance of 0.20 ± 0.03 rad (CCC-E049). The data at both claimed scales lie within 1σ, with no evidence of anomalous clustering (CCC-E050). This adopts the panel's upgrade: the measurement is directly recorded. Confidence is moderate because only 100 simulations and the top 30 points were used, and the exact observed values sit in the claim wording rather than in the checked passages.

treatment.plainLanguage: The strongest hot spots are no more bunched together than chance would bunch them, contrary to a proponent suggestion that bunching would support CCC.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Refutes an optional proponent prediction; CCC never required the spots to cluster.
treatment.strongestObjection: Clustering confined to weaker points, or detectable only with more simulations, would be missed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A larger simulation set or a full-population test finding significant clustering

claimAssessments.reasoning: Bielewicz et al. conclude that the large-radius deficit is 'yet another manifestation' of the known anomalous large-scale distribution (CCC-E056), and trace the anomalous variances to the low-order multipoles (CCC-E057). Held at provisional against two seats that sought well supported. It rests on one paper; its conditioning result (CCC-C512) is held here on the paper's statement alone; and the low-multipole oddities are themselves unexplained.

treatment.plainLanguage: The sky's biggest-scale ripples, already known to be odd, explain why large rings look too quiet.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Gives a conventional cause for one feature proponents still cite; it does not reach the ellipse test.
treatment.strongestObjection: It relocates the oddity to an unexplained large-scale anomaly rather than removing it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent replication of the conditioning test
Conditioned skies that still lack the large-radius deficit

claimAssessments.reasoning: The same paper concludes that the clustering of low-variance rings in a few large regions indicates large-angular-scale features rather than randomly placed sources (CCC-E056, CCC-E057). Held at provisional against two seats that sought well supported. It rests on one paper, uses a different statistic from the 2020 triple-centre count, and has never been tested against that figure.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ring centres crowd into a few big regions because of the sky's large-scale pattern, not because of scattered sources.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The direct conventional rival to the supercluster reading of the centre crowding, not yet tested on the proponents' own statistic.
treatment.strongestObjection: Proponents read clustering as previous-aeon superclusters, which CCC may predict; clustering alone does not choose between the two readings.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The 2020 triple-centre count run on skies copying our largest-scale ripples

claimAssessments.reasoning: Penrose states the requirement and calls mass fade-out 'an admittedly unconventional hypothesis' (CCC-E015). Tod, CCC's chief independent mathematical developer, lists implementing it as an open question (CCC-E016). This adopts the dissent of three seats: every element is conceded by the theory's author and his closest collaborator. The 2025 conservation law (CCC-E022) is progress but supplies no fade-out mechanism. That no accepted mechanism exists also leans on the prior of electron stability.

treatment.plainLanguage: For CCC to work, every massive particle, even the electron, must eventually lose its mass, and no known physics does that. Penrose admits it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A theoretical cost that weighs on CCC's plausibility but says nothing about the sky features.
treatment.strongestObjection: With a positive cosmological constant, mass is not fixed by the relevant symmetry group, so fade-out may be less exotic than it sounds.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A field-theoretic fade-out mechanism consistent with electron stability
A no-go theorem ruling fade-out out

claimAssessments.reasoning: No checked record supports the reset; the claim's source is cited without a checked passage. Eckstein argues that information loss raises global quantum entropy, undermining the renormalisation the crossover needs (CCC-E017), and Tod treats the surrounding questions as open (CCC-E016). The incumbent's 'mixed' implied support that the record does not hold. It is not graded contradicted: this is one analysis in a live quantum-gravity dispute, using a notion of entropy Penrose does not adopt. The balance tilts against the claim, leaning on priors about unitarity.

treatment.plainLanguage: CCC needs each new universe to start tidy. Whether its bookkeeping allows that is disputed, and the one detailed analysis says no.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Answers CCC's own motivating question; failure would hurt the theory, not the sky claims.
treatment.strongestObjection: Eckstein's refereed argument (CCC-E017) stands unanswered by any analysis on the other side.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent derivation of the entropy reset
A second analysis confirming Eckstein's result

claimAssessments.reasoning: Penrose introduces gravitation-only particles of about a Planck mass, decaying with a lifetime of 'perhaps something like' 10^11 years, and raises whether their decays might be detectable by LIGO (CCC-E018). Held at well supported against two seats that sought established. The parameters are hedged, 'decay completely within an aeon' is an inference, and Allen's work (CCC-E070, CCC-E071, CCC-E072) constrains detectability, not the content of the prediction.

treatment.plainLanguage: CCC says dark matter is made of very heavy, gravity-only particles that slowly decay: a real, forward-looking prediction.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: States what CCC commits to rather than evidence for it; any test runs through detectors.
treatment.strongestObjection: No decay spectrum or rate is computed, so the prediction is hard to test.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A computed decay channel and event rate
A detector signal matching them

claimAssessments.reasoning: Penrose states 'there is no inflation in CCC' and assigns the near scale-invariant fluctuations to erebon decay in the previous aeon (CCC-E018). This adopts the dissent of three seats, since the claim describes the theory in its author's words. BICEP/Keck's r < 0.036 (CCC-E021) leaves the discriminating measurement open. The mechanism has not been shown to reproduce the measured spectrum.

treatment.plainLanguage: CCC drops cosmic inflation and says the early universe's pattern of ripples came from decaying dark matter in the previous universe.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Sets up the one test where CCC is exposed: a primordial gravitational-wave detection would count against it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Tod asks whether 'inflation before the Bang' can be made sense of, so the framing may shift.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A confirmed detection of primordial gravitational waves in the microwave background's polarization
A derivation of the measured spectrum from erebon decay

claimAssessments.reasoning: As worded, the claim records Penrose's proposal, which his note states (CCC-E019, CCC-E064). This adopts the panel majority; the incumbent's 'contradicted' graded the conjecture rather than the claim. The conjecture itself is in poor shape: after subtracting a maximum-likelihood waveform, Nielsen et al. find no significant residual correlation (CCC-E067), and Allen's memory background misses detectability by 35 orders (CCC-E069). The premise (CCC-E062) and a 2026 extension (CCC-E077) are context only.

treatment.plainLanguage: Penrose suggested that odd correlated noise at LIGO might be decaying dark-matter particles. He did; the noise largely vanishes on a better analysis, and the signal would be far too weak.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A true report of a proposal; the proposal's failure (CCC-E067, CCC-E069) weighs only on the erebon route.
treatment.strongestObjection: A non-spherical decay or a nearby galactic source has never been calculated.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An emission mechanism giving a computable strain at a detector
Correlated noise found at the time delay of a nearby galaxy, as Penrose proposed

claimAssessments.reasoning: Allen's refereed calculation gives Ω_GW(25 Hz) < 2 × 10⁻¹⁰³ for Planck-mass particles with lifetimes beyond the Hubble time decaying to two gravitons, about 95 orders of magnitude below the LIGO O1+O2 limit (CCC-E042). Held at well supported against three seats that sought established. It is a single calculation, conditional on its model, and has not been independently reproduced.

treatment.plainLanguage: A calculation shows that the gravitational-wave hum from such decays would be vastly too faint for LIGO to hear.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Closes the detector route under the emission Penrose described; says nothing about erebons as dark matter.
treatment.strongestObjection: It assumes a homogeneous population and isotropic decay; local concentrations and anisotropic emission are not modelled.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A decay model with anisotropic emission that yields detectable strain
